title: Latency crediting — econ bench runbook
content:
Objective:
Short narrative of the experiment runbook and early findings for the latency-crediting idea. This is a working draft — lots of TODOs and rough numbers. Goal is to produce a concise bench collateral piece (text + ascii charts) we can hand to Product/Optimize and Console for framing next-phase experiments and a small eng spike.

Motivation / framing:
- Observability + Optimize teams have been exploring how small SLO relaxations can unlock batching/tiling opportunities without materially hurting UX. 'Latency crediting' is a lightweight policy: give request classes a small 'credit' (ms) of extra p99 headroom that can be consumed by opportunistic packing, prefetch backoff, or tiling to reduce GPU slots used per second.
- Hypothesis: For typical session mixes, 10–40ms of targeted crediting yields 8–25% cost savings on token amortized spend while p99 degrades within acceptable bounds for most interactive flows.

High-level design (policy sketch):
- Each route / tenant / SLA-tier attaches a credit budget (ms) and a consumption policy (soft vs hard).
- Scheduler attempts to group or delay non-critical tokens if the request has credit remaining.
- Credits are replenished per session or per minute depending on route.
- Fallback: if batching would cause downstream p99 > (SLO + credit) then decode runs immediately (no credit use).

Experiment matrix (what we ran):
- Workloads: (A) short-turn chat (user prompt 8–40 tokens + 35–120 gen tokens); (B) micro-embeddings burst (20k qps small batches); (C) multi-turn assistant sessions (context priming + variable gen lengths).
- Model: open-Llama-70B-ish quantized (Q4) on a 4xA100 equivalent slot (representative internal dev config).
- Scenarios: baseline (no credits, strict SLO enforcement), credit-10ms, credit-25ms, credit-40ms.

Test harness / telemetry captured:
- p50, p90, p95, p99 latencies (end-to-end from request receive -> last token sent)
- tokens/sec per GPU, slot occupancy, average KV cache hit rate
- amortized $/k-token (internal cost model) and relative cost change vs baseline
- error/fallback count (requests that refused credit and ran fast-path)

Representative results (abridged, smoothing applied; numbers are averages across 3 x 30m runs):

ASCII chart: normalized cost vs p99 (lower cost good, lower p99 good). Baseline normalized cost=1.00

Scenario     | normalized-cost | p99-ms
-------------------------------------
baseline     | 1.00            | 118
credit-10ms  | 0.92            | 129
credit-25ms  | 0.82            | 156
credit-40ms  | 0.76            | 204

Interpretation notes:
- Small credits (10ms) provide modest cost wins (~8%) while p99 rise is small (~+11ms). Good candidate for conservative tiers.
- Mid credits (25ms) hit a cost sweet spot for sessionized workloads (amortization allowed additional tiling). Cost down ~18% with p99 +38ms; acceptable for many product flows with visible loading indicators.
- Large credits (40ms) continue to reduce cost but p99 penalty grows non-linearly; more fallbacks and visible tail jitter observed in UX probes.

Breakdown by workload type (high level):
- Short-turn chat: best win around credit-25ms; high callback rate to fast path for credit-40ms because micro-interactions are latency-sensitive.
- Embeddings bursts: marginal win — embeddings throughput dominated by batch sizing already; crediting only helps when admission control is limiting concurrency.
- Multi-turn sessions: biggest savings since tiling/prefetch can collapse repeated context work and amortize startup energy.

Telemetry snippets (sessionized):
- Slot occupancy: baseline 63% avg -> credit-25ms 78% avg (fewer idle gaps)
- KV hit-rate: small uplift (3–6%) driven by slightly longer overlap windows
- Fallbacks (per 10k reqs): baseline 0, credit-10ms 120, credit-25ms 420, credit-40ms 980

User-facing risk matrix (first-pass):
- Visible UX regressions: medium after 25ms depending on route (must pair with streaming indicators or progress tokens).
- Error amplification: low — policy is additive and falls back to baseline decode when it would exceed budget.

Operational considerations:
- Instrumentation: need per-request credit usage counters (credit-consumed-ms), rejection reasons, and percentile shift dataset by route and tenant.
- Rollout strategy: start with internal tenants + non-customer-critical demo routes. Canary via Console with per-tenant toggle and per-minute credit cap.
- Monitoring: create p99 delta alarms and a "credit-burn" cost dashboard to correlate credit consumption with $/k-token.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to set initial credit budgets automatically? (proposal: small ML model or rule-of-thumb map by average prompt+gen length)
- Should credits be dynamic (replenish faster during sustained low-load)?
- UX: experiment with streaming-first behavior vs single final chunk to mask p99 shifts.
- Evaluate across other model families (decoder-only vs encoder-decoder) and quantization levels — quantization can change decode shapes and thus the cost vs latency curve.

Immediate next steps (owners):
- Quick spike: replicate credit-25ms test on 2 more model configs (Ethan Ross) — due 2029-06-24.
- Console feature proto: per-tenant credit toggle + burn metric (Lina Gómez) — wireframe by 2029-06-21.
- Alerts: add p99-delta alarm prototype for credited routes (Sofia Patel) — staging by 2029-06-20.

Appendix: small ascii microchart showing cost curve vs credit size (points are scenario averages):

Credit-ms -> normalized-cost
[0] 1.00 |###########
[10]0.92 |#########  
[25]0.82 |######     
[40]0.76 |#####      

Notes to self / rough transcript bits:
- Keep this doc as bench-to-collateral seed; want a single slide + one-pager with the ascii table and recommended guardrails.
- Need UX team signoff for any >25ms default credit for public traffic.
- Ticket OBS-7421 contains raw traces and benchmark scripts (bench/crediting/).

End.
